items.name: narration_en
items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy geography story video for BHUGOL, a popular geography fun-facts YouTube channel. The Narrator is thrilled to be telling you this: bursting with energy, a hyped, super-excited host, bright and very expressive, like an excited friend who can't wait to show you something amazing. Big smile in the voice. Wide, lively pitch movement: rise with real curiosity on every question, say every number with a genuine 'WOW', and land each punchline with a grin after a tiny comic pause. The ONE exception is the line about the people who died in the 1900 hurricane: say that single line lower, slower and with respect, no smile, then lift the energy straight back up on 'fought back'. The line 'But the storm isn't what finished it' is whispered-excited, like sharing a secret. The first line ends on a punchy, curious 'Why?'. The last line trails off unfinished on 'Either way, that's why...', voice staying up, so it loops straight back into the first line. Pace is quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, short crisp pauses; never slow, flat, calm, sleepy or documentary-serious. Accent: native General American English narrator, neutral American accent from the first word to the last. VOICE IDENTITY: always the same warm baritone host, same person and same energy level throughout. Pronounce 'Galveston' as 'GAL-vis-tun', 'Houston' as 'HYOO-stun', 'bayou' as 'BY-oo', 'Spindletop' as 'SPIN-dul-top'.
lines: Narrator
America's biggest port is fifty miles from the sea. Why?
Narrator
The city actually on the coast is little Galveston.
Narrator
But in eighteen eighty, Galveston was the biggest city in Texas.
Narrator
And Houston? A muddy town on a shallow bayou.
Narrator
So how did Houston steal the crown?
Narrator
September eighth, nineteen hundred. A hurricane hits Galveston.
Narrator
The island's highest point: under nine feet. The storm surge: over fifteen.
Narrator
At least six thousand people died. Still America's deadliest natural disaster.
Narrator
Galveston fought back. A seventeen-foot seawall... and it raised the whole city.
Narrator
But the storm isn't what finished it.
Narrator
Four months later, oil erupts at Spindletop.
Narrator
Oil companies wanted a port no hurricane could wash away.
Narrator
So Houston dug its bayou into a ship channel. Fifty miles long.
Narrator
In nineteen fourteen, the President pressed a button in Washington... and a cannon fired in Houston.
Narrator
Ocean ships sailed right past Galveston.
Narrator
Today: Houston, two point four million people. Galveston? About fifty-three thousand.
Narrator
Now it's just Houston's beach town.
Narrator
So... genius, or just lucky? Either way, that's why...
